lecture: L23) Ocular manifestations of systemic diseases.txt
expansion:
A. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca is correct. The lecture states that dry eye in rheumatologic conditions is “referred to as keratoconjunctivitis sicca” and that the most common causes include “Sjögren syndrome, SLE, and rheumatoid arthritis” (L23, page 33). Thus, Sjögren syndrome with chronic bilateral irritation and burning is the course-supported diagnostic association. The gritty foreign-body sensation, Schirmer wetting of less than 5 mm after 5 minutes, and punctate epithelial erosions support aqueous-deficient dry eye with ocular-surface epithelial damage (not taken from the course material).

B. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is an allergic ocular-surface disorder, classically dominated by marked itching and often associated with giant tarsal papillae and/or limbal disease, rather than Sjögren-associated tear deficiency (not taken from the course material). The course labels vernal keratoconjunctivitis and shows its characteristic clinical images, but does not provide this clinical distinction in text (L6, slide 38).

C. Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis produces focal inflammatory phlyctenules at the conjunctiva, limbus, or cornea, rather than bilateral aqueous-deficient dry eye caused by Sjögren syndrome (not taken from the course material). The course names phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis but does not state its cause, symptoms, or diagnostic differentiation in text (L6, slide 46).

D. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is an acute, highly contagious adenoviral conjunctivitis, typically with watery discharge, follicular conjunctivitis, and possible preauricular lymphadenopathy, not a chronic Sjögren-related dry-eye syndrome (not taken from the course material). The course covers viral conjunctivitis but does not name epidemic keratoconjunctivitis or adenovirus (L6, slide 34–36).
objective: Recognize Sjögren syndrome as a common cause of keratoconjunctivitis sicca.
